chapters.title: Chapter 4: Trading Forex Legally in India

lessons.title: Currency Options Basics: Calls, Puts and Premiums on USD/INR

children.text: Farooq, the Pune importer, has an $80,000 payment due next month. Futures would lock his rate at about 95.95, which protects him if the rupee crashes. But if the rupee strengthens to 94.50, he is stuck paying 95.95 while his competitors pay less. He wants something closer to insurance: protection if USD/INR shoots up, and the freedom to benefit if it falls. That is exactly what a USD/INR call option gives him, for a price paid upfront. This lesson explains calls, puts, strikes and premiums, and shows how Indian importers and exporters use them to cap their worst-case rate without giving up the upside.

body.text: A futures hedge locks your rate in both directions. An option hedge sets a worst-case rate and leaves the better outcomes open. The premium is the price of that flexibility, and like any insurance, it is paid whether or not you end up needing it.

children.text: Calls, Puts, Strikes and Premiums

markDefs.definition: An option giving the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy the base currency at the strike price. A USD/INR call gains when USD/INR rises above the strike.
An option giving the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to sell the base currency at the strike price. A USD/INR put gains when USD/INR falls below the strike.
The fixed exchange rate written into an option contract, at which it is settled against the reference rate at expiry.
The price the option buyer pays the seller upfront. For USD/INR options it is quoted in rupees per dollar.

call option

put option

children.text: Farooq's Call: Insurance Against a Weaker Rupee

USD/INR is around 95.80. Farooq buys 80 lots of the monthly 96.00 strike call at a premium of ₹0.45 (illustrative). His total premium is 0.45 × $1,000 × 80 = ₹36,000, paid upfront. At expiry, if the reference rate is above 96.00, the call pays him the difference. If it is below, the call expires worthless and he simply buys dollars at the cheaper market rate.

body.latex: \text{Call payoff per dollar} = \max(S_T - K,\ 0) \qquad \text{Put payoff per dollar} = \max(K - S_T,\ 0)
body.caption: S_T is the reference rate at expiry and K the strike. Subtract the premium to get profit or loss.

body.title: Farooq's premium
body.prompt: Farooq buys 80 lots of the 96.00 USD/INR call at a premium of ₹0.45. What is the total premium he pays, in rupees?
body.explanation: Premium = 0.45 × $1,000 × 80 lots = 0.45 × 80,000 = ₹36,000. This is his maximum possible loss on the option, whatever happens to the rupee.

body.caption: Long USD/INR 96.00 call bought at ₹0.45. The loss is capped at the premium below 96.00; above 96.45 the call makes money, offsetting Farooq's rising rupee cost for his dollar payment.
Farooq's $80,000 payment with the 96.00 call bought at ₹0.45 (premium ₹36,000, ignoring other costs)

body.title: Farooq's worst-case rate
body.prompt: With the 96.00 call bought at a premium of ₹0.45, what is the highest effective USD/INR rate Farooq can end up paying for his dollars, ignoring other costs?
body.explanation: Worst-case rate = strike + premium = 96.00 + 0.45 = 96.45. Above 96.00 the call pays back every paisa of the extra cost, so his rate never goes higher than 96.45. Below 96.00 he pays the market rate plus 0.45.

body.title: Farooq's Effective Rate: Unhedged vs Futures vs Call Option

children.text: Read the chart carefully. If the rupee weakens a lot, futures give Farooq the best rate, 95.95 against the option's 96.45. If the rupee strengthens, the option wins, because he keeps most of the benefit. Neither hedge is better in every outcome. Futures trade away the upside for a certain rate. Options pay a premium to keep the upside.
Priya's Put: A Floor for an Exporter

Priya, the Coimbatore exporter, is owed $150,000. She buys 150 lots of the 95.50 put at ₹0.40, paying 0.40 × $1,000 × 150 = ₹60,000. If the rupee strengthens below 95.50, the put pays the difference, so her effective rate never falls below 95.50 minus 0.40 = 95.10. If the rupee weakens to 97.00, the put expires worthless, but she converts her dollars at 97.00 and ends up with an effective 96.60 after the premium.

body.caption: Long USD/INR 95.50 put bought at ₹0.40. It gains when the rupee strengthens below 95.10, protecting Priya's dollar receivable, and costs only the premium if the rupee weakens.

body.title: The put pays out
body.prompt: At expiry, the reference rate is 94.00. Priya holds 150 lots of the 95.50 put she bought at ₹0.40. What is the put's net profit after the premium, in rupees?
body.explanation: Payoff = (95.50 minus 94.00) × $1,000 × 150 = 1.50 × 1,50,000 = ₹2,25,000. Net of the ₹60,000 premium: ₹1,65,000. Her $150,000 converts at 94.00 into ₹1,41,00,000, and adding ₹1,65,000 gives ₹1,42,65,000, an effective rate of exactly 95.10, her floor.

children.text: In, At or Out of the Money

body.title: What makes a premium expensive or cheap

markDefs.definition: The part of an option's premium equal to what it would be worth if it expired now. Zero for out-of-the-money options.
The part of an option's premium above its intrinsic value, reflecting the chance of a favourable move before expiry.

children.text: Every premium has two parts.
Intrinsic value
is what the option is worth right now.
Time value
is what you pay for the chance of a bigger move before expiry. Time value rises with:
More time to expiry.
A three-month option costs more than a one-week option at the same strike.
Higher expected volatility.
Before RBI policy, a US Fed decision or during a crude spike, premiums jump because big moves are more likely.
The forward premium.
Because USD/INR forwards trade above spot, calls tend to cost more than puts at the same distance from spot.
A practical implication: the time to buy insurance is before the storm. Hedgers who wait until the rupee is already sliding usually pay much higher premiums.

columns.label: Futures hedge
points: No upfront cost beyond margin, which is returned
Locks one rate in both directions
Best when you want certainty and the budget is fixed
You give up gains if the currency moves your way

columns.label: Option hedge (buying)
points: Pays a premium upfront that is not returned
Sets a worst-case rate, keeps the better outcomes
No margin calls for the buyer
Best when you want protection but also flexibility, such as when a tender may not be won
Costs more when volatility is high

body.text: Selling options looks like easy money because most options expire worthless and the seller keeps the premium. But the seller's losses can be many times the premium when the rupee moves sharply, as it did in 2013, 2022 and 2026. For rupee-pair options, positions must also relate to a genuine currency exposure, so writing USD/INR options just to earn premium is not a permitted use. Beginners hedging a business exposure should stick to buying calls or puts.

body.title: Pick the right option
body.question: A Kochi seafood exporter will receive $60,000 in one month. She wants protection if the rupee strengthens sharply, but wants to benefit if the rupee weakens. Which hedge fits best?
options: Sell 60 lots of USD/INR puts to collect premium
body.explanation: An exporter is hurt when USD/INR falls. A bought put pays off in exactly that case and sets a floor, while leaving her free to convert at a better rate if the rupee weakens. Calls protect importers. Selling puts adds risk instead of removing it. Buying futures would add to her dollar exposure rather than hedge it.

body.title: The tender that may not happen
body.scenario: A Nagpur engineering firm has bid for a contract to supply equipment to a buyer in Kenya, priced at $200,000. The result of the tender will be announced in six weeks. If the firm wins, it will receive the dollars about two months after that. USD/INR is 95.80. The firm's CFO is considering three choices: (1) sell 200 lots of USD/INR futures now, (2) buy 200 lots of a 95.50 put for ₹0.40, or (3) do nothing until the tender result.
body.prompt: Evaluate each choice, including what happens if the firm loses the tender, and recommend an approach. Consider the exposure rule, the cost of each hedge and the risks.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Futures now: if the firm wins, the rate is locked near the futures price. But if it loses the tender, it is left with a short USD/INR position and no dollars coming in. That is an open speculative position, with MTM losses if the rupee weakens, and it no longer has a genuine exposure behind it.
2. Buying puts: the cost is known, 0.40 × $1,000 × 200 = ₹80,000. If the firm wins and the rupee strengthens, the floor is 95.10. If it loses the tender, the most it can lose is the ₹80,000 premium, and there are no margin calls. The expiry must be matched to the likely payment date, or rolled later.
3. Doing nothing: costs nothing now, but if the rupee strengthens sharply before the result, the contract becomes less profitable, and premiums may be higher by the time the firm hedges.
4. Exposure rule: a bid is an anticipated exposure. The firm should document the tender and check with its broker and bank that the hedge is treated as legitimate. It must not keep a hedge running if the exposure disappears.
5. Recommendation: for an uncertain exposure like a tender, buying options is usually the better fit, because the premium is a fixed, known cost and the firm is never left holding a large open futures position if the deal falls through. Once the contract is won, it can decide whether to switch to a futures or forward hedge for the confirmed amount.

body.title: Option style
body.textWithBlank: USD/INR options on Indian exchanges are ___-style options, which means they can only be exercised at expiry.
body.explanation: European options settle only at expiry, against the reference rate. American options, common in US equity markets, can be exercised any time before expiry.

cards.definition: The right to buy the base currency at the strike. Gains when USD/INR rises. Used by importers to cap their cost.
The right to sell the base currency at the strike. Gains when USD/INR falls. Used by exporters to set a floor.
The upfront price of an option, quoted in rupees per dollar for USD/INR. The buyer's maximum loss.
The part of the premium above intrinsic value, higher with more time to expiry and higher volatility.

points: A call gives the right to buy dollars at the strike and gains when USD/INR rises. A put gives the right to sell and gains when USD/INR falls.
USD/INR options on Indian exchanges are $1,000 lots, European style, with premiums in rupees per dollar and cash settlement against the reference rate.
An importer buying a call caps the cost at strike plus premium. An exporter buying a put sets a floor at strike minus premium.
An option buyer's maximum loss is the premium, with no margin calls. Sellers post margin and face much larger potential losses.
Futures lock a rate both ways; options set a worst case and keep the upside for a premium.
Premiums rise with time to expiry, volatility and, for calls, the USD/INR forward premium.
Options suit uncertain exposures such as tenders. Rupee-pair options, like futures, must relate to a genuine currency exposure.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, trading or hedging advice. Premiums, strikes and outcomes in the examples are illustrative and ignore brokerage, taxes and other costs. Rupee-pair options may be used only in line with RBI's rules on genuine currency exposures. Contract details can change, so check the latest specifications with NSE, BSE and your broker, and consult a qualified adviser before hedging business exposures.
